mainProgression.description: The riff implies a i-III-IV movement typical of minor key rock, with the single-note melody outlining these chord tones

sectionProgressions.description: The iconic riff is a single-note melody played on the low A string, transposed down an octave by the pitch-shift effect to sound like a bass line
Power chords support the vocal with the riff continuing underneath, building on the minor tonality
The chorus expands harmonically with a wider chord palette, creating tension and release through the descending C5-B5 movement

harmonicFunction: E5 (i) - Dark, powerful tonic center anchoring the riff and verse sections
G5 (III) - Major mediant adding brightness and upward harmonic motion
A5 (IV) - Subdominant providing the primary harmonic contrast
C5 (VI) - Submediant creating a dramatic pre-resolution moment
B5 (V) - Dominant chord resolving back to the E5 tonic

techniques.name: Single-Note Riff with Octave Effect
techniques.description: The signature technique of the song: a simple single-note melody played on the A string, processed through an Electro-Harmonix POG octave pedal to produce a bass-like tone an octave below

notes: The riff is played entirely on the A string (5th string)
Learn the note sequence of the main riff
Learn the fret positions for each note in the riff
Jack White used an Electro-Harmonix POG to shift the pitch down one octave
Without the octave pedal, the riff can be played on the low E string for a similar bass effect
Alternative low E string version: the riff notes - D(10th fret or open D) - the riff notes
sequence: Place index finger at 7th fret of A string for the E note
Pick the note twice (E-E) with even quarter-note rhythm
Slide or shift to 10th fret for G note
Return to 7th fret E, then descend: 5th fret D, 3rd fret C, 2nd fret B
The B note is held longer before the riff repeats
tips: Use your index finger as a guide along the A string surface
Let each note ring clearly before moving to the next
Focus on the rhythm - the notes are simple but the timing must be precise
If you don't have an octave pedal, try playing on the low E string for a heavier sound
Keep unused strings muted with your fretting hand to avoid noise
details.progression: E - E - G - E - D - C - B (single notes on A string)

techniques.name: Power Chord Verse Rhythm
techniques.description: During verse and chorus sections, the riff transitions to power chords providing a fuller harmonic foundation beneath the vocals

notes: E5: 0-2-2-X-X-X (Open low E + 2nd fret A and D strings)
G5: 3-5-5-X-X-X (3rd fret low E + 5th fret A and D strings)
A5: 5-7-7-X-X-X (5th fret low E + 7th fret A and D strings)
C5: 8-10-10-X-X-X (8th fret low E + 10th fret A and D strings)
B5: 7-9-9-X-X-X (7th fret low E + 9th fret A and D strings)
Use steady downstrokes for a driving, heavy feel
sequence: Start with E5 open power chord for verse sections
Shift to G5 at 3rd position for contrast
In the chorus, move through G5 - A5 - E5 - C5 - B5
Return to the single-note riff between sections
tips: Keep power chord shapes consistent as you move up the neck
Mute higher strings by lightly resting your index finger across them
The transition from single-note riff to full power chords should be seamless
Use downstrokes throughout for consistency with Jack White's aggressive style
details.progression: E5 - G5 - A5 for verse; G5 - A5 - E5 - C5 - B5 for chorus

techniques.name: Slide Technique (Riff Variation)
techniques.description: An optional slide technique that can be applied to the main riff for a smoother, more connected sound between notes rather than discrete fret-to-fret movement

notes: Use slides to connect the notes smoothly
Use slides to connect the notes smoothly
Continue the slide down from 3rd to 2nd fret for C-to-B
Slides add a vocal, expressive quality to the riff
sequence: Play the note at the correct fret position, then slide finger up to 10th fret G
Return to 7th fret E with a fresh pick attack
Pick the note, then slide down to 3rd fret C
Slide to the final note of the phrase
tips: Maintain even pressure during slides to keep the note ringing
Don't lift your finger off the string during the slide motion
The slide-up to G should be slightly faster than the descending slides
Practice the slide motion independently before incorporating into the full riff

sections.name: Main Riff (Intro)
sections.description: The instantly recognizable single-note riff that has become one of the most iconic melodies in modern rock, played on one string with an octave-down effect
notes: Entire riff played on the A string (5th string)
Quarter-note rhythm with the final B held slightly longer
The octave pedal gives it the bass-like quality heard on the recording
Without the pedal, playing on the low E string gives a heavier approximation

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: The verse layers power chords over the continuing riff, with aggressive strumming supporting the vocal melody
notes: Power chords provide the harmonic foundation under vocals
The riff continues underneath played by a separate guitar or bass
Strong downstrokes maintain the aggressive energy
Simple i-III movement keeps the focus on the vocal melody

sections.name: Chorus
sections.description: The chorus expands the harmonic palette with a wider chord progression, building intensity with the G5-A5-E5-C5-B5 movement
notes: More chord changes than the verse, creating harmonic interest
The C5 to B5 descending movement creates dramatic tension
B5 resolves strongly back to E5 when the riff returns
This section has the most energy in the song

sections.name: Breakdown / Guitar Solo Section
sections.description: The song strips back to the raw riff before building into an aggressive, feedback-laden guitar section with distorted power chords
sections.progression: E5 riff - E5 - G5 - A5 (building intensity)
notes: Starts with the riff stripped down to create tension
Gradually adds distorted power chords to build intensity
Jack White uses feedback and aggressive picking in this section
Builds dynamically to the final chorus repeat

alternatives: Any electric guitar with a thick, dark tone
guitar.pickup: Neck humbucker or single-coil for the warm, fat riff tone; bridge pickup for aggressive chorus sections

amp.recommended: Fender Twin Reverb (or similar clean amp driven hard)

settings.bass: 7 (fat low end to support the octave-down riff)

effects.distortion: Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi for fuzz/distortion sections
effects.other: Electro-Harmonix POG (Polyphonic Octave Generator) - essential for the octave-down riff effect; alternatively, a Digitech Whammy or Boss OC-3 can approximate the sound

beginner.focus: Learn the single-note riff on one string and basic power chord shapes
steps: Memorize the riff note positions on the correct string
Practice the riff slowly with a metronome at 80 BPM
Learn E5, G5, A5, C5, and B5 power chord shapes
Build up to 124 BPM maintaining clean note separation

intermediate.focus: Combine the riff with power chord sections and learn the full song structure
steps: Practice transitioning from single-note riff to power chords
Learn the verse and chorus progressions at full tempo
Work on dynamic contrast between sections
Play through the complete song structure without stopping

advanced.focus: Recreate the authentic tone with effects and master the aggressive performance style
steps: Set up the octave pedal effect for authentic riff tone
Add distortion/fuzz for the heavier sections
Master the aggressive picking dynamics Jack White uses
Work on the breakdown section with feedback and intensity control

commonMistakes: Playing the riff too fast without maintaining rhythmic precision
Not letting each note ring clearly before moving to the next
Forgetting to mute unused strings, causing unwanted resonance
Making the power chord transitions too abrupt instead of smooth
Ignoring the dynamic contrast between quiet riff and loud chorus sections
practiceRoutine: Warm up with single-note exercises on the A string for 5 minutes
Practice the riff at 80 BPM with clean note separation
Work on power chord shapes and transitions for 10 minutes
Practice the full riff at increasing tempos (90, 100, 110, 124 BPM)
Play through the entire song structure with backing track
focusAreas: Clean single-note articulation on the A string
Rhythmic precision - the riff must be locked to the beat
Smooth transitions between single-note riff and power chord sections
Dynamic control for building intensity through the song
String muting to keep the tone clean and focused
metronomeWork: Start at 80 BPM playing the riff with quarter notes
Add the descending portion of the riff at 90 BPM
Practice power chord changes at 100 BPM
Build to 110 BPM with full song sections
Target 124 BPM for authentic full-speed performance
